title: Gravity and orbits
scope: Choose the objectives in your school’s topic list. These are original practice questions with illustrative values, not a claim of an official school paper format.

objectives.label: Explain and use universal gravitation.
objectives.note: Masses attract each other gravitationally; for spherical masses outside one another the inverse-square model uses centre-to-centre distance.

objectives.label: Explain and use orbit.
objectives.note: An orbit is a continually deflected path under gravity, combining inward acceleration with motion around the attracting body.

objectives.label: Explain and use elliptical orbit.
objectives.note: In an elliptical orbit, the attracting central body lies at one focus, not generally at the geometric centre.

objectives.label: Explain and use measuring g.
objectives.note: A laboratory measurement of gravitational attraction can determine the gravitational constant used with orbital and surface measurements.

objectives.label: Explain and use prediction and evidence.
objectives.note: A physical model is strengthened when its predictions match new observations.

objectives.label: Explain and use mission trajectory.
objectives.note: A spacecraft trajectory is chosen subject to fuel, timing and gravitational constraints.

cards.definition: Masses attract each other gravitationally; for spherical masses outside one another the inverse-square model uses centre-to-centre distance.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Why is an astronaut’s apparent weightlessness not proof that gravity is absent? Gravity is present in a nearby orbit. The astronaut and spacecraft fall together, so there is little supporting contact force.
cards.confusion: Gravity does not end at the edge of the atmosphere.
cards.question: Explain universal gravitation from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Masses attract each other gravitationally; for spherical masses outside one another the inverse-square model uses centre-to-centre distance. Gravity does not end at the edge of the atmosphere.

cards.definition: An orbit is a continually deflected path under gravity, combining inward acceleration with motion around the attracting body.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: In a circular orbit, does a satellite’s velocity remain constant? Explain. No: its direction changes continuously. It can have constant speed while its velocity changes.
cards.confusion: An orbiting satellite does not require a continuous outward force to cancel gravity.
cards.question: Explain orbit from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: An orbit is a continually deflected path under gravity, combining inward acceleration with motion around the attracting body. An orbiting satellite does not require a continuous outward force to cancel gravity.

cards.definition: In an elliptical orbit, the attracting central body lies at one focus, not generally at the geometric centre.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Compare a planet’s speed close to the Sun and far from it in a fixed elliptical orbit. It moves faster near the Sun. It moves more slowly farther away, consistent with equal areas swept in equal times.
cards.confusion: An ellipse’s focus is different from its centre.
cards.question: Explain elliptical orbit from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: In an elliptical orbit, the attracting central body lies at one focus, not generally at the geometric centre. An ellipse’s focus is different from its centre.

cards.definition: A laboratory measurement of gravitational attraction can determine the gravitational constant used with orbital and surface measurements.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Explain how measuring a small gravitational force in a laboratory can help estimate Earth’s mass. The laboratory experiment determines G. Combine G with measured surface gravitational acceleration and Earth’s radius using the gravitational model.
cards.confusion: A balance experiment is not a direct reading of the entire Earth’s mass.
cards.question: Explain measuring G from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A laboratory measurement of gravitational attraction can determine the gravitational constant used with orbital and surface measurements. A balance experiment is not a direct reading of the entire Earth’s mass.

cards.definition: A physical model is strengthened when its predictions match new observations.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: The observed position of a planet differs slightly from a simple two-body prediction. Suggest a physical refinement before abandoning gravity. Include gravitational effects from other planets. The two-body approximation leaves out these additional interactions.
cards.confusion: A successful prediction supports a model without establishing that every detail is exact.
cards.question: Explain prediction and evidence from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A physical model is strengthened when its predictions match new observations. A successful prediction supports a model without establishing that every detail is exact.

cards.definition: A spacecraft trajectory is chosen subject to fuel, timing and gravitational constraints.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Does a spacecraft need its engine firing throughout a coast between burns? Explain. No: its motion continues and gravity changes its trajectory during coasting. Engines are used for particular planned changes of velocity rather than to sustain motion itself.
cards.confusion: A longer route is not necessarily a mistake if it reduces a mission’s required propulsion.
cards.question: Explain mission trajectory from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A spacecraft trajectory is chosen subject to fuel, timing and gravitational constraints. A longer route is not necessarily a mistake if it reduces a mission’s required propulsion.
